speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on Friday,
June 15, the minister answered a question of mine with regard to the relationship between the War Veterans Allowance Act and the new old age pension legislation, and I quote from his answer as recorded on page 4136 of Hansard:
The matter referred to in the question asked on Tuesday by my hon. friend is being reviewed and considered at the present time.
I rise to express the hope that that review and consideration may result in a decision by the government to bring in an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act at the fall session of parliament. In my view it is urgent that it be done not later than that so that any changes made in the War Veterans Allowance Act can be made effective at the same time as the changes to be made with respect to old age pensions. As the minister knows, there are a number of problems that will arise out of this change affecting veterans, on the one hand, and so far as those from 65 to 69 years are concerned, affecting also the provinces.
It is not sufficient simply to say to a veteran that he has a choice between the War Veterans Allowance Act and the old age pension. In many cases the veteran feels that he would rather be under the War Veterans Allowance Act, particularly if he is between the ages of 65 and 69, because he feels there is a measure of entitlement under that act which he has earned through his war service and which does not exist under the other act. That is one aspect that I need not go into any further, but it does call for consideration. From the standpoint of the provinces, there is the feeling that veterans, who are a federal government responsibility, should not simply be pushed over on to them even if it is only to the extent of 50 per cent of the cost entailed.
There is also the matter of treatment and hospitalization rights which are enjoyed by veterans who qualify for the war veterans allowance. There may be cases where the monetary benefits would seem to be to the advantage of the veteran who transferred to the old age pension, but he will be in quite a dilemma if that means the loss of his treatment and hospitalization benefits. That is another aspect of the problem that will have to be gone into.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
Then there is the question of the older veteran with the younger wife. At the present time a married veteran who qualifies for the war veterans allowance gets the married rate regardless of the age of his wife. If a veteran were over 70 with a wife 63 or 64 years of age, or of any younger years, and he went over to the old age pension, there would be nothing for his wife, as matters now stand. These are problems that have to be looked at even if one only takes the position that the war veterans allowance recipient must not be allowed to suffer any loss by reason of the change that is taking place.
The minister assured me of that in the answer he gave on June 15, and I know that that is a matter of concern to the government, as it is to all of us. But I do emphasize the fact that there should not be any gap, that any changes to be made in the War Veterans Allowance Act should be made so that they can come into effect on January 1. If they are not dealt with now they should be dealt with in the fall session, without fail.
Having said that, may I point out that there are many who feel, as I do, that it is not sufficient just to make amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act that will protect the position of the veteran and keep it at what it now is. The fact of the matter is, and this is one of the exceptionally good things about the changes being made in our old age pension legislation, that after January 1 a great many Canadians, in fact some 72 per cent of all those 70 years of age and over will have an improvement in their financial position. Sixty per cent of those 70 years and over are not getting any old age pensions now and they will get $40 per month. Another 12 per cent of those 70 years of age and over are now getting old age pensions but at reduced rates and they will draw the full amount of $40 per month. Those who will benefit will include retired judges, retired civil servants and so on, because for all those 70 years of age and over the old age pension legislation will have no means test attached to it.
But if all these others are to gain from the changes being made, so should our burnt-out pensioners. Although there is no means test in the old age pension legislation for those 70 years and over, many of those receiving the burnt-out pension will be affected by the fact that there is a means test under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Unless some change is made many of these war veterans allowance recipients 70 years of age and over will not have their position improved by the enactment of the old age pension legislation.
Not only should there be the necessary amendments to make sure that the veteran does not lose his treatment or hospitalization

552. Gallantry awards-world war II, $18,000.

This vote covers gallantry
awards for world war II. Is there any way in which similar payments can be made to the men who were decorated in world war I?

Before the minister answers, may I recall the case of Captain Edward Bellew of Chase in Kamloops constituency, who was completely destitute? I drew the attention of the then minister, the late Ian Mackenzie, to the case, and through Walter Tucker he took advantage of a provision of the Pension Act for special meritorious service and granted a special award to Captain Bellew who distinguished himself during the first war. Therefore such a provision existed in the act before the second world war.

The assistance to which the
hon. member for Temiscouata is referring Is, I think, under section 21 of the Pension Act.
I do not know.

It is called the meritorious
pension. The point I am asking about is entirely different. It has to do with a payment that is made to those veterans who received awards for gallantry. Apparently the Canadian government pays all these men from world war II. What I am inquiring about is the position of the men who were decorated with the Victoria Cross, the distinguished conduct medal or the military medal during the first world war.

In the case of world war I
awards, those are paid by the United Kingdom government but no payment is made for the military medal. It was not done at the time, and it is not done by any British country. For world war II we have assumed payment of these awards since 1943.

Has any consideration been
given to making payments to the men of the first war who received the military medal?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
It has been a matter of
discussion, but none of the countries of the

commonwealth have assumed that responsibility. The British have for world war II but not for world war I, and that has been uniform throughout the commonwealth.

There cannot be very many
men living who won the military medal in world war I. Can the parliamentary assistant say how much would be involved?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No. It is not a large sum individually but no estimate has been made of it because so far there has been no agreement to do it. I think there would be difficulties in breaking it up since all the awards were made by the British in world war I. To initiate -a different practice in different sections presents difficulties.

Surely we awarded the
military medal to these men because they won it and not because some person in another part of the commonwealth is making an award. Surely we awarded it because these men were the recipients of a very outstanding reward for valour, the military medal. There can be no difference in the valour of the men who won it in the first war, and I believe that the people of Canada would be more than willing to reward them for the winning of this decoration for valour and would wish it to be payable to every man. Surely it does not make any difference in a man's contribution to his country whether it was made between 1914 and 1918 or between 1939 and 1945. Talk about making flesh of one and fowl of the other! We are now practising that on the men of the armed forces. I do not think it would cost a great deal to remind the taxpayers that, according to the feeling of the government, they owe these men this recognition.
The award was not made to these men because of the fact that any other part of the British empire does or does not make this payment. Surely that was not the motive. The men in the last war won it for what they did in that war, and the men in the first war won it for the same reason. I think it should be applicable to all winners of the military medal who are Canadians and fought in the Canadian forces, irrespective of what may be done in any other part of the commonwealth. We should certainly stop making flesh of one and fowl of the other.

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to recipients of the Victoria Cross in the first world war. These men are paid in United Kingdom funds and they are Canadians. They have been in Canada for some years. They feel that they are being discriminated against because of the fact that, as I believe, we pay veterans
Supply-Veterans Affairs of the last war in Canadian funds. These men are paid in UK. funds and they lose a considerable amount of money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If I may interject, the British award is paid at the rate of five Canadian dollars for the British pound, and as you know the British pound is not worth $5 now.

I was talking to one of these men the other day and he made that complaint. As a matter of fact he made representations to me because he thought that perhaps I could bring it up. He said he was losing some amount each year which I have forgotten because of the fact that he is paid in U.K. funds.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Probably the gentleman to whom the hon. member refers earned his V.C. when he was serving with the British army and not with the Canadian army.
That is true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is a British award to British soldiers, and what I said a moment ago would not apply. But Canadians who won the Victoria Cross with the Canadian services are paid at the rate of five Canadian dollars for each British pound in the award.
Is there any way the situation of that man could be corrected and he could be paid on a par with others in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We have nothing to do with awards to British soldiers.
But he is still a Canadian who served in the British army. He was a Canadian to start with, and still is.

I should like to know whether the amount in British money that goes with the award is deducted from the pension of any war veteran; and I will illustrate my point. Some years ago I was informed that at Christie Street hospital in Toronto there was a disabled veteran who had been awarded the Victoria Cross who was receiving a pension of $40 a month. He had to pay for his board $30, which left him $10 a month for pocket money. According to what I heard the pension commission took from his pension the amount of $40 that he was receiving at the time for his Victoria Cross, so there were four months for which he had no pocket money just because he was the recipient of the highest decoration within the commonwealth. I told the minister of the time, who was the late Ian Mackenzie, that I did not know if it was true but to check it and deny it if it was not true. He never denied it. Therefore I hope that when disabled men receive awards they will not be deducted from the amount of their pensions.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
The answer to my hon. friend's question is that any payment connected with the award of a medal is not considered as income with regard to either pension or war veterans allowance.
Then that is an improvement over past policy.
We are improving all the time.
What is the position with regard to the winner of a Distinguished Conduct Medal in both wars?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The gratuity is $100, with a corresponding addition for each bar.
$100 a year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No; it is a gratuity of $100, or 12J cents a day if he is a pensioner.
Is that the same for the men of both wars?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It only came into effect in world war II.
I am very glad the minister says conditions in the department are improving all the time. I knew that; that was why I spoke as I did this afternoon.

The minister said the government keeps on improving; no doubt it is slow but sure. I would like him to explain why the veterans of the first war who won these awards have not been given these gratuities. Was it felt that the men who were given the awards in the first war for some reason or other did not merit these gratuities? I would like an explanation by the minister, to see whether or not we are improving.

My understanding is that at the time of the first war these medals were awarded by the British government and granted by His Majesty, and that the monetary award which accompanied them was paid and has continued to be paid by the British government. In 1943, during world war II, the responsibility of the British government was discharged in connection with these awards and we assumed the responsibility. That is where the difference comes in.
Did the British government make these awards of the D.C.M. and M.M. in the first war?

My statement was correct; awards in the first war were given by the British government. During the first war there was no monetary award attached to the Military Medal. That is the situation in all commonwealth countries, and that explains why there is a difference.

I knew about the difference; I knew these medals were given by the British government. Then this government came along and when they got a chance to really show their appreciation to these heroes they said we believe you are entitled to these awards for gallantry on behalf of the people of Canada, and we believe you are entitled to a monetary award in addition to the metal medal. We believe that is so as far as the second war is concerned, but not with respect to such awards in the first war. If the government believes that any Canadian winning these medals merits the monetary award, why should that not apply to the veterans of the first war as well? Would the minister say what might be done for the winners of the D.C.M. and M.M. in the first war as far as the monetary award is concerned, so they may be on an equal footing with the winners of those awards in the second war.

I have said that the winners of the D.C.M. do receive the award. As for the winners of the M.M., I must say I have not given the matter any consideration up to the present, but I will be very glad to consider my hon. friend's views.

554. Last Post fund, $135,000.
Will the minister say whether or not the regulations governing the administration of the last post fund are subject to revision by the Department of Veterans Affairs?

My understanding is that the last post fund is a voluntary organization which has a working arrangement with the department. We make grants for the burial of indigent veterans, but the fund as such is an independent organization and its bylaws are not under the control of the department.
Is it not true that this fund is given a grant by the federal government?
Yes; I have said that we do make grants on the basis of the number of burials of indigent last post fund veterans looked after.

There are some cases which perhaps do not receive as careful consideration from the fund as one might expect. I had one such case which I brought to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. It was settled satisfactorily, I think; at least I have heard nothing more about it. In this case a veteran who lived in Drumheller was out of employment. He was given a ride to Edmonton on a truck; while going into Edmonton there was an accident and he was killed. One of the businessmen in Drumheller, out of his own pocket, paid the

expenses of having the body returned to Drumheller. The widow, of course, was left penniless and had no means whatever of getting this body returned to Drumheller. This man paid that money out of his own pocket. Then when the veterans organization in Drumheller appealed to the fund to have the burial expenses-which, if I recall the figure rightly, amounted to about $110-paid for by the fund, they objected on the grounds that they had not been notified and that, had they been notified, the body would have been buried on the spot where it fell, something which was an absurdity. It fell on the highway. From the very fact that that body had been moved one foot from where it fell, I presume they take the view that the federal government, the Department of Veterans Affairs or anyone else had no right to suggest to them what they should or what they should not do.
I want to say that with the kind co-operation of the parliamentary assistant in bringing this matter to the attention of the proper authorities the thing was settled satisfactorily. But it seems to me that those in charge of the fund should be a little bit more considerate of those people whom they are serving; and that in such a case as that, it should never have been necessary for me to bring the matter to the attention of anyone in the federal government. The very fact that the federal government makes a contribution to that fund is in itself sufficient reason, I think, that they should exercise some power of suggestion at least over those in charge of this fund in order to see that it is properly administered.

From the point of view of a kitchen garden, it will adequately supply him with all the vegetables he needs for his household. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a suggestion and also a vigorous complaint under this heading of Veterans Land Act administration. We all realize that settlement under the Veterans Land Act has been of great benefit to large numbers of veterans in Canada, and it has been of benefit to a considerable number in my constituency, particularly under the small holdings section. But I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that while the $6,000 loan was generally satisfactory when the act was adopted, it is now insufficient owing to the rising cost of living or the decreasing value of the dollar, whichever you might call it, for the settlement of veterans in small holdings in some cases and definitely so in connection with small farms or full-scale farming.
I have had a good number of complaints from veterans in my constituency and veterans in surrounding constituencies. I happen to have here a resolution that was adopted by the veteran settlers of Lakeview Heights Veterans Land Act project in the Okanagan valley, and I just want to read one paragraph of it because in that one paragraph I think they make a good case. I might say that the whole presentation on the part of these veterans is carefully prepared and is

Supply-Veterans Affairs substantiated with facts. In this brief they say this, and I shall simply read one paragraph:
The problem of the veteran settler has been progressively increased by the shrinking value of the country's medium of exchange. The present cost of construction, according to figures appearing in the 1950 report of the society of residential appraisers, as at 15 October, 1950, is 65-5 per cent higher than in 1946, and 135 per cent higher than in 1939. Reference to V.L.A. figures published in the Vancouver Province January 18, 1951, shows that in the lower mainland of B.C. there has been a total of 535 homes built under the V.L.A. in the five years, 1946-1950. These have been built at an average cost of $7,009 . . . Building costs are continuing to rise. The cost of building in 1946, according to the 1950 report of the society of residential appraisers, was $6'32 per square foot; in 1950 it was $8.75; and quotations from local contractors are now in excess of $9 per square foot.
That is a situation which is growing worse from year to year. I think the present $6,000 loan is insufficient. I would urge the minister to give consideration to the serious situation existing with regard to small-holdings developments, owing to the lack with regard to the amount of the basic loan.
In addition to that, I just want to have a word or two to say about the Veterans Land Act administration as it applies to my constituency. I usually have happy relations with all the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs; and, like the minister, I was somewhat indignant when I heard the hon. member for Temiscouata speak this afternoon. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not make a complaint or support a complaint unless I think it is founded on sound grounds. In Kootenay West for some years there was a regional office established in Nelson which served the east and west Kootenay district. It was under Mr. Dodding who died two or three years ago. He did good work indeed. He had a good knowlege of the district, was well liked by the veterans, and made every possible effort to settle men on farms in the area and on small holdings. The veterans of the district are extremely sorry that he suddenly passed away. Since Mr. Dodding's decease the Veterans Land Act administration have seen fit to remove the administration from Nelson and put it under the supervision of the supervisor in Kelowna. Mind you, Kelowna is in a different type of country, and they are dealing with problems not of the same nature as we have them in the Kootenays.
Owing to the economy drive which the government initiated last fall I understand that the Department of Veterans Affairs, like other departments, have been asked to reduce staff.	In Kootenay West we had
three field men covering the whole area- all of them good men. Finally the superintendent, on the recommendation of the
[Mr. Herrldge.l
supervisor at Kelowna-I do not think, Mr. Chairman, it was entirely without bias- dismissed Mr. Green, the senior veteran in the government's employ, with six years in the department and nearly thirty years' residence on the north shore of Willow Point, and a man who had given excellent service to the veterans of the district. So indignant were the veterans of Kootenay West at his dismissal that every branch of Kootenay West has written me about it, and some 50 other veterans. Here was a man who was giving excellent service. He was a veteran of two wars, and he was resident in the district and a farmer and had six years' service with the department itself.
I want to point this out to the minister. On occasion after occasion decisions made by Mr. Green in his office in each of the Kootenays were vetoed by someone higher up and then later, on re-investigation, were O.K.'d. I remember last year Mr. Baldwin, who was for a term acting district superintendent of Vancouver, came into the district because of complaints from veterans, men who wanted to buy a small holding on the north shore near Willow Point, an excellent buy, a five-room modern house, four acres of ground, water piped in all directions, fertile land, for $4,000 cash. The regional office in Kelowna turned the offer down. Mr. Baldwin, the acting superintendent at that time, came into the district and looked at the house for only a few minutes, and wrote to me to say that any veteran who wished to purchase the place could do so because the department considered it a satisfactory buy. But the veteran who was interested in the place had been waiting for four months, and by that time he had left the district in order to find other suitable accommodation.
I suggest that the minister give some consideration to this, because I believe it is a justifiable complaint. We have a great opportunity for small holdings in our district, particularly for the men working in the plants of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
As a result of the dismissal of this senior official we have two men left, excellent -men, Mr. Mackie doing the east Kootenay area and Mr. Cooper the west Kootenay area. Both of these men are doing the best they can. Both are overworked because of the distance. These two men have to serve a population of 70,000 people; that is to say, the veterans in a population of 70,000 people. They are serving a country of 20,000 square miles in area, and they are working in a district that produces the greatest wealth per capita of any district in Canada, according to the publication "Business Week".

I am making a plea for a little more activity on the part of the Veterans Land Act administration so far as the Kootenays are concerned. There are hundreds of men in my district who would welcome a small holding if they could obtain one. One of the big handicaps has been this two acres or nothing business. It is difficult in our district to get two acres of cultivable land close to Nelson. Surely half an acre is sufficient for any man working in an industrial plant where he is making his wages and is using his small holding as a place to grow some vegetables, keep a few chickens, a pig and so on. I ask the minister and his department to give consideration to that. I do urge that the minister and the officials of the Veterans Land Act administration review the situation. I am not blaming altogether those in charge at Kelowna. They have very serious problems to attend to. They have some difficult conditions, and they have to motor over from Kelowna some hundreds of miles into our valley to service applicants, and so on.
Under the present arrangements the Nelson office is open for four hours every week on Saturday afternoon, I think, for veterans who wish to make application for small holdings or full-time farming or for veterans who wish to make their payments. Imagine a man driving from Edgewood to Nakusp to Nelson, a distance of 165 miles, to see a person who is in an office that is open for four hours. If he has a flat tire be misses his appointment. That is not good enough service for such a great wealth-producing area as that.
I may say that when I return home I speak to a lot of organizations,' such as boards of trade, Rotary clubs, Kiwanis clubs, veterans and labour organizations and so on. I am going to do all I can to mobilize public opinion in Kootenay West to see that we get a better deal so far as veterans settlement is concerned.
Before concluding I want to draw to the minister's attention the fact that I have a report here addressed to the minister from Mr. Baldwin at the time that he was acting superintendent-at least, I have a copy of the report. He deals with construction in the Kootenays. For this whole area he says:
Construction supervisor Nield has supervised construction of seven new houses in both Kootenays during 1950. In 1949 the total was also seven.
When the regulations were changed from half an acre to a minimum of two acres to the value of $500 I have personal knowledge of 245 applications that could not be processed because of the change in those regulations. If the regulations were changed there
Supply-Veterans Affairs are dozens and dozens of men who would wish to settle under the small-holdings sections. We have some excellent small holdings settlements there, but there is a great demand from others who have not had the opportunity up to date. As far as the interior of British Columbia is concerned, I would urge the minister's department to give it very serious consideration. I do ask the minister personally to look into what I consider-not only myself personally, but all the veterans organizations of Kootenay West and a large number of responsible citizens-the gross injustice that was done a veteran of two wars who had served the country and the veterans of the district so well.

I should like to endorse the request which has been made by the hon. member for Kootenay West that there be a regional office opened in the city of Nelson or that some better arrangement be made for looking after the veterans in the Kootenay district. It so happens that I was born in the Kootenay district and I know the country well. Everything that he has said is absolutely correct. It is quite inefficient to try to supervise that district from the Okanagan district which is several hundred miles away across two mountain ranges. To get from Kelowna to Nelson you have to cross those ranges. The hon. member for Kootenay West has made a very reasonable presentation of this situation and I would ask that the minister have the whole question investigated.
I will be very glad to take the matter up with the director.

In saying a few words on small holdings I should like to follow up what the hon. member for Wentworth said. In my riding many more veterans would have built houses provided they could have built within the town limit and on smaller holdings. To buy two acres adjacent to a town or village costs as much as a smaller holding would, or a quarter or half acre would cost him within the town. Therefore many veterans have not built their own houses. They are still renting houses or looking to the government to help them.
I think the greatest asset in the country is to have people who own their own homes. When a man owns his own home he feels he has a stake in the country that he has not in any other way. Every dollar he spends on that house is his. If he spends it on a rented house or in the house that he happens to occupy he looks upon it as a lost dollar. I think it is a big mistake to try to hold veterans down to try to build a house on two acres. I know some veterans

Supply-Veterans Affairs in my riding who have built on two acres of land. They have had to go out of the town half a mile or a mile, and pay more money for their two acres than a nice little lot in town, perhaps a quarter or half acre, would have cost. Everyone who knows anything about land knows that a quarter of an acre, with a proper home built on it, with a good lawn and garden, requires plenty of care. I doubt whether the minister or the parliamentary assistant or many of the officials in the department know what two acres of land is. If one gave them a few sticks and a hammer and told them to go out into a ten-acre or twenty-acre field and stake out two acres they would not be within 25 per cent of being correct.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
This brings up once again the question which has run through this legislation from the beginning. Small holdings were designed to be ancillary to the Veterans Land Act, and as such when you get below the prescribed area you are getting into what is in effect urban housing, rather than land settlement.
The decision that may have to be taken some day-certainly it has been reviewed over and over again in the light of representations which come from smaller industrial cities particularly, and some of the cities in those areas which are heavily industrialized-is whether or not the department is going into the business of urban housing. That is what it amounts to, when you reduce it below the given amount.
Until now the decision has always been that the justification for small holdings was the relationship to land settlement. In those areas, the inception of the idea was to get


certain groups of veterans away from congested areas in cities into larger areas where they could get homes comparable to those available in cities but at very much lower prices, and at the same time to give them a backlog of security through the productivity of their land.
Owing to the fact that the scheme came into being at a time when everybody everywhere was gravely concerned with the question of housing itself, this question has cut across all decisions. Back in September, I believe it was, of 1946, when the government began, under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to build rental housing restricted to veterans in various urban areas throughout the country, the decision was taken that to make the differential more clearly defined between them, those having small holdings would have to move out to larger areas, and get larger areas of land.
Up to the present time there has been no change. The department is continuing to settle on uncompleted projects veterans on half-acre holdings, and veterans with 50 per cent pensionable disability or more are still eligible for half-acre settlement. But there is no proposed change at the present time. I think this question which keeps coming up from time to time may ultimately have to be settled along the lines I have indicated.
How many are still under the British family scheme who are continuing to make payments, and what is the amount of the indebtedness still owing under that scheme?
As at March 31, 1951, there remained 463 active accounts for British families.
How much was owing on those?
As of March 31, 1951, it was $601,195.36.

What is the chance of getting a contract with or selling some bacon to Great Britain this year?

with Britain that if there is any bacon available at the price offered, it will be purchased for them. But at the present time there is no indication that there will be any bacon available. The price is about ten cents higher than the British price offered would permit of our paying.

Not to our knowledge. No
offers have been made of any higher price; not to my knowledge. It is just possible that if we had any to sell and if we were to attempt to sell it to the British, we might be able to get a higher price than they offered some time ago. But we are consuming the pork as fast as it is being produced and put on the market.

How much pork has been
exported to the United States?

Very little. It is a negligible quantity. It is only an amount which goes across for certain purposes. We get just about as much back for other purposes. On balance, we might say that there is nothing at all passed over to the United States.

Will the minister tell the
committee why it is that we are not producing any more pork than we are producing? Surely in a country like Canada we should be able to produce pork for export. What would be the reason why we are not producing as much as we were producing in 1944?

The producers in Ontario,
for example, are producing as much as they ever produced. They are producing as much in Quebec, generally speaking, as they ever did. The place where the pork is not being produced is largely in the prairie provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Manitoba is down as well. The only time when we were producing any considerable amount more than we are producing now was during the wartime, in the middle of the war. At that time we were not able to sell our grain. We wanted cash, so we fed even wheat to hogs to get cash. For example, in Saskatchewan, where there has been as big a drop as anywhere, we were producing about four times as many hogs in the middle of the war as we are producing now. The only reason for that is the fact that we prefer to produce grain on the prairies and to sell it rather than to feed it, if we can sell the grain. We are selling all the grain at the present time. There is no difficulty, as there was during the war, to find a market for the grain. It is being sold; and we are selling it rather than feeding it. That is a choice we make out there under these circumstances. I do not know that there is much that could be done about it.
Are we selling the frozen wheat to greater advantage than, we could sell it through hogs?

I do not think so. On my
own farm I am feeding frozen wheat; but many of my neighbours are not doing so. 
In western Canada we seem to prefer to sell feed rather than to feed hogs under these circumstances; and that is what we are doing. I am not arguing whether it is right or wrong. The farmer himself makes that choice. Some farmers go on feeding hogs and others do not.

Is there any possibility
that the prices for hogs are not sufficiently high or that there is not sufficient stability in the price?

There is. I do not think
there is any question about that. Hogs have been selling at a much higher price than anyone ever anticipated. If you start to figure what you could make by feeding wheat to hogs, you will find that you can get considerably more by feeding it to hogs. But our people prefer to sell the wheat at the present time. They make a fairly good return out of it and they are selling it.

A few minutes ago the
minister mentioned this frozen wheat or low-grade wheat. Is the situation not that the price of the wheat has been higher, relatively, than the price of barley, with the result that anybody in the hog business would much prefer to buy barley-and did so- and feed it to hogs than to buy wheat?

That is true. As long as
there is barley available, the farmer prefers to feed barley. But there is not a sufficient volume of barley to take care of all the requirements and they feed wheat.

I think that is probably going to be one of the difficulties in getting rid of this wheat. The food value per pound in relation to the price you have to pay for it is not as great as the food value per pound of barley for which you pay a lower price. It would seem to me that if we are going to get rid of this low grade wheat through feeding it to hogs it is probably going to be necessary that the price of it be brought down so that it will be more comparable with the price of barley.

The difficulty of that is that the low grade wheat is selling higher proportionately than the high grade wheat at the present time. The present indications are that a higher final payment will be made on some of the lower grades than will be made on the higher grades. There is quite a demand for feed, and that is one of the reasons why they sell it.

I should like to ask the minister this question. Is it not the situation that we have a large amount of this low-grade wheat in elevators and that, as a matter of fact, it is to a considerable extent

clogging what you might call our wheat handling facilities at the present time?

speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Of course the hon. member is rather outside my department; but nevertheless it is the old question. The bidding for the low grade wheat is high and I do not know how you are going to get the price down while other people are bidding the price up. They are offering more for the wheat in order to get it.
Who wants to get the price down?

The minister has not
answered my question at all. Is it not the situation that our handling facilities-our elevators and so on-are actually to quite an extent clogged with this wheat because people have not bought it at the prices it is being sold at?

My understanding is that there is a considerable amount of wheat in elevators largely because they have not been able to get cars to ship it out. I hope the minister is right.
